en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 57.
The Training Rule on Bathing:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the bhikkhus were bathing in the Tapodā.

At that same time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, thinking, "I shall bathe my head," went to the Tapodā and waited to one side, thinking, "I will wait until the venerable ones have finished bathing. The bhikkhus bathed as long as it was still dark.

Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having bathed his head at an improper time and stayed outside the city because the city gates were closed, approached the Blessed One early in the morning with his ointment still unabsorbed.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “For what reason, Great King, have you come so early, with your ointment still unabsorbed?”
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha [was addressed] by the Blessed One...
Instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by a discourse on the Dhamma, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One,
circumambulated him with his right side toward him,
and departed. Then, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that even upon seeing a king, the monks bathe without knowing moderation?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, even after seeing the king, bathe without knowing moderation?
This, monks, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:"
“Whichever bhikkhu, however, should bathe within half a month, it is an offense of expiation.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, during the heat and the season of feverish distress, the bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not bathe; they lay down with their limbs covered in sweat.
“Even the robes and the lodgings become soiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One said:
“Monks, I allow you to bathe at intervals of no more than half a month during the time of heat and the time of fever.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whatever monk should bathe within half a month, except at the proper time, it is an offense entailing expiation.

Herein, this is the proper time: when there is a month and a half remaining of the hot season, and the first month of the rainy season—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of fever; this is the proper time therein."
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were ill.
The monks who were visiting the sick said this to the sick monks:
“Is it bearable, friends? Is it sustainable?
“In the past, friends, we used to bathe within half a month, and because of that we were comfortable.
But now, thinking ‘It has been forbidden by the Blessed One,’ we do not bathe out of scruples, and because of that we are not comfortable.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow, monks, a sick monk to bathe at intervals of less than half a month.
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:..."
“Whosoever bhikkhu should bathe within half a month, except on the proper occasion, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Herein, this is the proper occasion: when one and a half months of the hot season remain, and the first month of the rainy season—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of feverishness, and the time of illness; this is the proper occasion therein.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, having performed building work, the monks, being scrupulous, did not bathe.
They lay down with their limbs covered in sweat. Their robes and lodgings became soiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, to bathe at intervals of less than half a month during the time for ritual acts.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
‘Whosoever monk should bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except on the proper occasion, it is an offense of expiation.’”

"In this regard, this is the occasion: 'When one month and a half of the summer remains,' and 'the first month of the rainy season'—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of feverish distress, the time of illness, and the time for work; this is the occasion therein.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, having traveled a long distance, the bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not bathe.
They lay down with their limbs covered in sweat. Their robes and lodgings became soiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One said:
“Monks, I allow you to bathe at intervals of less than half a month during the time of traveling on a journey.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whatever monk should bathe within half a month, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation.
Herein, this is the proper time: the remaining one and a half months of the hot season and the first month of the rainy season—these two and a half months."
"The time of heat, the time of feverish distress, the time of illness, the time of work, and the time of traveling on a journey—this is the occasion there.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, several bhikkhus were doing robe-work in the open air and were covered by a dusty wind; and the sky was sprinkling with rain drop by drop.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not bathe; they lay down with their limbs wet, and their robes and lodgings became soiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. …pe…
“I allow you, monks, to bathe at intervals of less than half a month during the season of wind and rain.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
‘Should any monk bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except on the proper occasion, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”

In this regard, this is the proper occasion: "When one month and a half remains of the summer, and the first month of the rainy season—these two and a half months are the time of heat, the time of feverish distress, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a journey, and the time of wind and rain; this is the proper occasion therein.
As for the phrase "but whoever":
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Less than half a month" means less than half a month.
"Should bathe" means:
If she bathes with powder or with clay, for each act there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
At the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Except at the proper time.
Except at the proper time.
"The hot season" means when one and a half months of the summer remain.

The time of feverish heat (*pariḷāha-samaya*) refers to the first month of the rainy season; during these two and a half months, it is said, "This is the time of heat, the time of feverish heat," and one may bathe.
The time of illness (*gilāna-samaya*) refers to...
If one is not at ease without bathing, it is a time for bathing when one is ill.
A "time for work" means even when the surrounding area has been swept; it is a time for bathing because it is a "time for work."
The occasion of traveling on a journey is as follows:
one may bathe thinking, "I will go two yojanas"; one may bathe while going; and one may bathe after having gone.
The occasion of wind and rain is as follows:
The monks are covered by a dusty wind, or two or three drops of water have fallen upon their bodies. Thinking, "It is a time of wind and rain," they bathe.
If it is less than half a month and they perceive it as less, and they bathe except at the proper time, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If it is less than half a month and they are doubtful, and they bathe except at the proper time, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If it is less than half a month and he perceives it as more, except on an appropriate occasion, and he bathes, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is more than half a month and he perceives it as less, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If it is more than half a month and he is uncertain, there is an offense of wrongdoing.
If it is more than one and a half months and he perceives it as more, there is no offense.
There is no offense at the proper time.
He bathes once every half-month;
he bathes more frequently than once every half-month;
he bathes while crossing over to the other side.
In all border regions, in times of calamity,
for one who is insane,
"For one who is a first-offender":
thus ends the seventh training rule concerning bathing.
